File: ./chapters/intro.tex

Tensor Networks allow the efficient representation and computation of quantum states for large $N$ using methods such as DMRG. Symmetric Tensor Networks yield a speedup over traditional methods for [29]
appropriate Hamiltonians. [31]
Furthermore, we would also like to represent \emph{Anyonic} states and Hamiltonians by these operations, and since some anyon species are universal for quantum computation, we would like to represent circuits as well. It is folklore that tensor networks and quantum systems in general are goverened by category-theoretic constructions. [79]
[79]
In this thesis we give a formal overview how all these concepts fit into the same categorical [96]
framework while presenting a review of the existing literature, i.e. we give an interpretation of the results of \textcite{singhTensorNetworkStates2012a,weichselbaumTensorNetworksNumerical2012,pfeiferSimulationAnyonsTensor2010,dissertation,devosTensorKitjlJuliaPackage2025}% Missing ayeni, bultnick? maybe kirchner, read that. [119]
, embed them with a rigorous categorical theory and provide missing proofs. Due to the interconnectedness with topological order, we phrase them in the language of \cite{kongInvitationTopologicalOrders2022b}. [144]
[144]
\subsection{Thesis Outline} [2]
[2]
In \cref{sect:background} we review the technical literature which is shared by the chapters (sections?). We give accounts on symmetries, representation theory, fermionic networks, anyons and categories. \Cref{DecompositionOfSemisimpleCategories} presents the main theorem that is the backend of our tensor system. While we will state the first $2$ sections with scarce proofs, chapter \cref{???} will be quite rigorous and supercede all statements from the previous sections. [63]
[63]
Maybe we will present a outlook on Modular Categories [72]
[72]

\begin{literature}[\bf Tensor Networks] [0]
 The modern theory of \emph{tensor networks} shaped out of the study of \emph{renormalization} [13]
  and quantum many-body systems, initially with the \emph{density-matrix-renormalization-group} of \textcite{whiteDensityMatrixFormulation1992,whiteDensitymatrixAlgorithmsQuantum1993} and later extended by \textcite{ostlundThermodynamicLimitDensity1995} as a variational method (ansatz?) in the form of \emph{matrix product states} (MPS) (Maybe this is actually due to \cite{fannesFinitelyCorrelatedStates1992}). This was further generalized to 2 dimensions with the introduction of \emph{projected entangled-pair states} (PEPS) \cite{verstraeteRenormalizationAlgorithmsQuantumMany2004}. \emph{Multiscale-entanglement renormalization ansatz} (MERA) \cite{vidalClassQuantumManybody2008} can be considered as an extension of MPS allowing for long-range entanglement (this is probably wrong). Whats missing? Holography \cite{singhHolographicSpinNetworks2018} but there are earlier ones. [91]
[91]
  In the purely mathematical view as a network of tensor contractions however, both concept and the notation we use today were introduced by \cite{Penrose1971Applications} under the name of \emph{tensor-systems}. [119]
\end{literature} [119]
[119]
While we introduce this concept classically and endow it with symmetry as a start, we will start concerning ourselves with a categorical embedding of tensor networks in what is commonly reffereed to as a \emph{fusion-category} (Lit ???). [155]
[155]
\begin{literature}[\bf Symmetric Tensor Network] [155]
 Originally, the idea to exploit symmetries of the hamiltonian for a speedup was proposed to be used in dmrg by \cite{mccullochNonAbelianDensityMatrix2002} (What is \cite{sierraDensityMatrixRenormalization1998a}? This sounds like it as well.). More general theory for \emph{globally invariant tensor networks}, i.e. networks that are built of tensors that are globally invariant is given by \textcite{singhTensorNetworkDecompositions2010a} preceeding more detailed accounts on abelian symmetries \cite{singhTensorNetworkStates2011} and nonabelian ($\SU{2}$) symmetries in \cite{singhTensorNetworkStates2012a}. A similar approach to (non)abelian symmetries is given by \textcite{weichselbaumNonabelianSymmetriesTensor2012, weichselbaumXsymbolsNonAbelianSymmetries2020}. These rely on the general idea, that under representations of some compact group $G$, there are on site symmetries on each tensor, i.e. $[A, U_g^{\otimes k}] = 0$ there is a generalized \emph{wigner-eckart-theorem} for tensors with $n$ legs of the form [267]
  \[ [268]
    T \in \bigoplus_a D_a \otimes V_a [268]
  \] [268]
  where $D_a$ is a matrix and $V_a$ is a \emph{fusion-tree}, i.e. a clebsch-gordan tensor. [282]
  Reviews and specific algorithms in the SU(2) case are given by \cite{schmollBenchmarkingGlobal$SU2$2020, schmollTensorNetworkSimulations2020, schmollProgrammingGuideTensor2020}. [294]
  \cite[§~8]{schmollProgrammingGuideTensor2020} proposes that this method is appropriate for Anyonic simulation as well (although this is done earlier by singh \& pfeiffer.). [314]
  Symmetries as categorified networks, as we will present in \cref{chap:?}, are explained in \cite{dissertation} [326]
 and \cite{devosTensorKitjlJuliaPackage2025} and in this work in \cref{sect:Anyons}. [332]
[332]
  For a list of software implementing symmetries see \cref{app}. [340]
\end{literature} [340]
[340]
[340]
\begin{literature}[\bf{Anyons}]\label{Lit:Anyons} [340]
 \emph{Anyons} as quasiparticles with exotic exchange statistics were originally propsed by \cite{wilczek1990} \cite{leinaasTheoryIdenticalParticles1977a}. Anyons are usually described as \emph{defects} in a (topologically orderd?) medium of dimension two (technically codimension after \cite{SS23AnyonsInTedK}). [368]
  The exchange statistics of $N$ particles on this medium $M$ is goverend by the \emph{configuration space} [384]
  \[ [385]
    \mathrm{Conf}_N(M) = \{(x_1,\ldots,x_N) \in M^N : x_i \neq x_j \} \setminus S_N. [385]
  \] [385]
  The statistics of the particle exchange is given by the representation of $\pi_1(\mathrm{Conf}_N(M))$ (the fundamental (homology?) group). If $M = \R^2$, this corresponds to the \emph{braid group} on $N$ strands $B_N$. If the dimension of $M \geq 3$ this corresponds to the symmetric group $S_N$. If these representations are unitary and the (ground state?) is degenerate, this allows for \emph{topological quantum computation} (c.f. \Cref{lit:tqc}). [444]
\end{literature} [444]
[444]
[444]
[444]
\begin{literature}[Anyonic Spin Chains and Tensor Networks] [444]
 (Check if this is the first). A first appearance of \emph{Anyonic Tensor Networks} in terms of spin chains is given by \textcite{feiguinInteractingAnyonsTopological2007} as the \emph{golden chain}, which realizes a interacting $2$-local hamiltonian on a $n$ $\Fib$-anyon lattice. This is reviewed in \cite{trebstShortIntroductionFibonacci2008a} with generalizations to $3$-local and longer range hamiltonians. A general account outside of the $\Fib$-model can be found in \cite{gilsAnyonicQuantumSpin2013} and \cite{buicanAnyonicChainsTopological2017} (Check these again.). We can consider these approaches as a sort of manualization of the tensor network approach. Anyonic tensor networks are first introduced by \cite{pfeiferSimulationAnyonsTensor2010} and \cite{pfeiferSimulationAnyonsUsing2012}, developed out of the symmetry methods from \cref{sect:symmetricTensorNetworks} and both the \emph{isotopy} rules and anyonic operators defined in \cite{bondersonAnyonicEntanglementTopological2017}. Furthermore, stuctures such as an anyonic MERA are introduced. [561]
\end{literature} [561]

 Some (Many?) anyon theories are universal for quantum computation. \subsection{Tensors (Everything here is $fdVect_k$)} [5]
[5]
Generally, we want to regard a tensor as a thing equipped with legs, where each legs holds a vector space. But we also want to be able to regard tensors as operators such as Hamiltonians. [40]
[40]
Lets list some definitions of Tensor. A Tensor $T$ can be regarded as an element of a tensor product space [60]
\[ [61]
  T \in \bigotimes_{j \in J} V_j [61]
\] [61]
where each $V_j$ is a finite-dimensional vector space and we say $T$ is a $\left\vert J \right\vert$-legged tensor. [78]
[78]
Given !finite! dimensional Vector spaces $V$ and $W$, we have the identity that $V \otimes W^\ast \equiv Hom(W,V)$. This is called the \emph{hom-tensor duality}. (TODO: is this canonical? What about the other way around?) [108]
[108]
In a basis expansion, this would relate the expansion of $V \otimes W^\ast$ as [120]
\[ [121]
  T = \sum_{i}^{} v_i \otimes f_i [121]
\] [121]
where $f_i \in W^{\ast}  : W \to k$ with the map $T \in \Hom(W,V)$ as [128]
\[ [129]
  T = (w \mapsto \sum_{i}^{} f_i(w) v_i). [129]
\] [129]
[129]
[129]
Now, if we have a Tensor $T \in V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_n$, and since for any Vector space $V$, $(V^\ast)^\ast = V$, we can peel off any number of $V_{i}$s, take their duals and represent $T$ as a map [162]
\[ [163]
  T : V_{n}^\ast \otimes \cdots \otimes V_{k+1} ^\ast \to V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_k [163]
\] [163]
Note that we present the domain here in a contravariant fashion due to the contravariance of the dual. [181]
[181]
Lets look at an example, let $t \in V_1 \otimes V_2 \otimes W_{2}^\ast \otimes W_1^\ast$. We can represent as an operator in dirac notation: [197]
\[ [198]
  t = \sum_{i_1,i_2,j_1,j_2}^{} T^{i_1 i_2}_{j_1 j_2}  \ket{v^1_{i_1}} \ket{v^2_{i_2}} \bra{w^1_{j_1}} \bra{w^2_{j_2}} [198]
\] [198]
where $\ket{v_i}$ [200]
[200]
Graphically, we represent a general tensor [206]
\[ [207]
  T : (W_{n}^{\ast} \otimes \cdots \otimes W_1) \to (V_1 \otimes V_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_n) [207]
\] [207]
as follows, where we choose incoming arrows for duals in the domain and outgoings for normal spaces, and on the bottom we choose incoming for duals and outgoing for normals. [237]
[237]

Background in representation theory: [4]
[4]
\begin{definition}[Representation] [5]
 A representation of a group $G$ over a vector space $V$ is a group homomorphism [20]
  \[ [21]
    \rho : G \to \GL V, \quad \rho(g)\rho(h) = \rho(g \cdot h), \quad \rho(e) = id_V [21]
  \] [21]
\end{definition} [21]
We can state this equvalently as the representation under the group action of $G$ on $V$: [37]
\begin{definition}[Representation in action form] [41]
 Given a group $G$ and a vector space $V$, a representation is a map [55]
  \[ [56]
    \alpha : G \times V \to V, \quad (g,v) \mapsto g \cdot v [56]
  \] [56]
  such that this is linear, todo. I think we get the equality to the hom def if we set $g \cdot v = \rho(g)v$ [76]
\end{definition} [76]
[76]
\begin{definition}[Intertwiner] [77]
 A linear map $A : V \to W$ is an intertwiner, if under representations $\rho_V : G \to \GL(V)$ and $\rho_W \to \GL W$ it holds that [93]
  \[ [94]
    T \circ \rho_V(g) = \rho_W (g) \circ T \quad \forall g \in G [94]
  \] [94]
  we denote the space of all intertwiners as $\Hom_G(V,W)$. [103]
\end{definition} [103]
[103]
\begin{definition}[Unitary representation] [105]
 If our vector space $V$ is equipped  with a (Hermitian?) inner product [117]
\end{definition} [117]
[117]
\begin{definition}[Irreducible representation (Woit 16)] [121]
 A representation $\rho$ is an \emph{irrep} if there are no $W \subset V$ such that $(\rho_{\vert W}, W)$ is a representation. [138]
\end{definition} [138]
[138]
\begin{definition}[Tensor product representation] [141]
 Given reps $\rho_V$ and $\rho_W$, the \emph{tensor product representation} [150]
  \[ [151]
    \rho_V \otimes \rho_W : G \to \GL {V \otimes W} [151]
  \] [151]
\end{definition} [151]
[151]
\begin{definition}[Direct sum representation] [154]
 As above, the direct sum representation is a homomorphism [163]
  \[ [164]
    \rho_V \oplus \rho_W : G \to \GL {V \oplus W}, [164]
  \] [164]
\end{definition} [164]
[164]
\begin{definition}[Isotypic / Semisimple decomposition] [167]
 Each semisimple representation $V$ decomposes as [173]
  \[ [174]
    V \cong \bigoplus_{i \in I} V^{\oplus n_i} [174]
  \] [174]
  by grouping isomorphic simples. [178]
\end{definition} [178]
[178]
\begin{definition}[???] [178]
 Let $R_a$ and $R_b$ be two irreducible representation (spaces). Their tensor product is again semisimple and there is a decomposition [198]
  \[ [199]
    R_{a} \otimes R_{b} \cong \bigoplus_{c \in I} R_c^{\oplus N^{ab}_c}  [199]
  \] [199]
  where we call $N^{ab}_c$ the \emph{fusion multiplicty} in $G$. If $N_{ab}^c \leq 1$ for all $a,b,c$, we say that the representation is \emph{multiplicity-free}.  [220]
\end{definition} [220]
[220]
\begin{example}[Clebsch-Gordan series] [222]
 Let $G = \SU{2}$ and let $V_i$ and $V_j$ be two spin irreps of charge $i$ and $j$. These combine to [241]
  \[ [242]
    (\pi_{V_i \otimes V_{j}}, V_i \otimes V_j) = \bigoplus_{k \in \left\vert i - j \right\vert}^{i + j} (\pi_{V_k}, V_k) [242]
  \] [242]
\end{example} [242]
[242]
\subsection{Symmetric Tensors} [2]
[2]
%Here we want to define tensors that are invariant under a symmetry $G$ (a compact group). We say that a tensor $T \in () [2]
[2]
Let $G$ be a compact group. Consider a tensor $T$ living in the tensor product space of its legs: [21]
\[ [22]
  T \in V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_n \otimes W_m^\ast \otimes \cdots \otimes W_1^\ast [22]
\] [22]
[22]
Let $\rho_i : G \to \GL{V_i}$ be the linear representation of $G$ on each vector space $V_i$, and let $\sigma_j^\ast : G \to \text{GL}(W_j^\ast)$ be the dual representation on $W_j^\ast$. [44]
[44]
The total action of the group $G$ on the entire tensor product space is given by [60]
\begin{gather*} [60]
 \Pi: G \to \text{GL}\left(\bigotimes_i V_i \otimes \bigotimes_j W_j^\ast\right) \\ [61]
 \Pi(g) = \rho_1(g) \otimes \cdots \otimes \rho_n(g) \otimes \sigma_m^\ast(g) \otimes \cdots \otimes \sigma_1^\ast(g) [61]
\end{gather*} [61]
[61]
[61]
A tensor $T$ is defined to be a \textbf{symmetric tensor} (or $G$-invariant tensor) if it is invariant under simultaneous action on all legs for all $g \in G$ \cite{singhTensorNetworkDecompositions2010a}: [88]
\[ [89]
  \Pi(g) T = T \quad \forall g \in G [89]
\] [89]
[89]
Recall that by the isomorphism $\Hom(V,W) \cong W \otimes V^\ast$ as [96]
\[ [97]
  w \otimes f \mapsto (v \mapsto f(v)w). [97]
\] [97]
We can push the product representation through this isomorphism as [107]
\[ [108]
  \pi(g)(w \otimes f) = \rho_W(g)w \otimes \rho_{V^\ast}(g)f = \rho_W(g)w \otimes (\rho_V(g)^{-1})^T  f = \rho_W(g)w \otimes f(\rho_V(g)^{-1} ) [108]
\] [108]
\[ [109]
  \cong v \mapsto f(\rho_V(g)^{-1}v ) \rho_W(g)w [109]
\] [109]
[109]
By interpreting $T$ as a map [115]
\[ [116]
  T : W_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes W_m \to V_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes V_n [116]
\] [116]
it follows directly from the definition of global invariance that the tensor must commute with the group action and we get the following definition of a symmetric tensor: [144]
[144]
\begin{definition}[symmetric tensor] [146]
 \label{def:symmetricTensor} [146]
 A \emph{symmetric tensor} is an intertwiner of the representations of the group $G$: [159]
  \[ [160]
    \bigotimes_{j=1}^m \sigma_j(g) \circ T = T \circ  \bigotimes_{i=1}^n \rho_i(g) \quad \forall g \in G, [160]
  \] [160]
  which we denote by [164]
  \[ [165]
    T \in Hom_G(W,V). [165]
  \] [165]
\end{definition} [165]

\begin{corollary}[Networks of symmetric tensors are symmetric] [172]
 Since a tensor network is built by composition and application of the $(co)ev$ maps, both of which are intertwiners, the full network is also an intertwiner. Important there is that this entire discussion is only about FdVect or FdHilb for now, but i think the same applies to any braided category.    [223]
\end{corollary} [223]
[223]
\subsection{Review of Symmetric Tensor Networks.} [5]
[5]
The motivation for constructing symmetric tensor networks is as follows: Assume we have a (unitary) representation of a group $G$ denoted $U(g)$.  Furthermore assume we have a hamiltonian that commutes with $[U(g)^{\otimes L}, H] = 0$. If the ground state is unique, we can obtain [46]
\[ [47]
  U(g)^{\otimes L} H \ket{\psi_0} = H (U(g)^{\otimes L}) \ket{\psi_0} = E_0 U(g)^{\otimes L} \ket{\psi_0} [47]
\] [47]
and thus $U(g)\ket{\psi_{0} }$ is a ground state as well. By uniqueness [58]
\[ [59]
  U(g) \ket{\psi_0} = e^{i\theta(g)} \ket{\psi_0} [59]
\] [59]
[59]
\begin{figure}[h] [59]
 \centering [59]
 \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{../experiments/plots/su2_block_structure.pdf} [59]
  \caption{Three different presentations of the XXZ Hamiltonian. (i): In the default computational basis of spin vectors. (ii) In a reordering of the computational basis into equal spin up (down) classes, i.e. no spin up, one spin up etc..., here $U$ is simply a permutation matrix. (iii) After changing the basis into the $(S^2,S_Z)$ basis.} [113]
 \label{fig:diagonal_hamiltonians} [113]
\end{figure} [113]
[113]
\begin{definition}[XXZ-Hamiltonian] [114]
 \label{def:xxzHamiltonian} [114]
 The XXZ Hamiltonian on $N$ sites is [121]
  \begin{equation} [121]
  H [122]
    = [122]
    J \cdot [122]
    \sum_{i = 1}^{N} [122]
      (\sigma_i^x \sigma_{i+1}^x + \sigma_i^y \sigma_{i+1}^y + \Delta \sigma_i^z \sigma_i^z  ). [122]
  \end{equation} [122]
\end{definition} [122]
[122]
As given in \cref{def:xxzHamiltonian}, this acts on the \emph{spin basis} made of states $\ket{s_1 s_2 \ldots s_n}$ where $s_i \in \{\uparrow, \downarrow\}$. [137]
[137]
We can plot $H$ and realize the sparsity structure thereof. Furthermore, a suitable rearrangement induces a block structure \cref{fig:diagonal_hamiltonians}. [155]
[155]
Now, we can realize about this hamiltonian is that there is a symmetry with the representations of $\U 1$. Lets review this shortly. A representation of $U(1)$ is a group homomorphism [185]
\[ [186]
  \rho : \U 1 \to \GL V n , \quad \rho(e^{i\theta_1}) \rho(e^{i\theta_2}) = \rho(e^{i(\theta_1 + \theta_2)}). [186]
\] [186]
[186]
The XXZ model lives in the Hilbert Space $\mathcal{\MakeUppercase{H}} = (\C^2)^{\otimes n}$ and the relevant representation is generated by the total magnetization operator [206]
\[ [207]
  S^z_{\mathrm{tot}} [207]
  = [207]
  \frac12 \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \sigma_i^z [207]
\] [207]
The group action is given by [213]
\[ [214]
  U(\theta) [214]
  = [214]
  e^{-i\theta S^z_{\mathrm{tot}}}. [214]
\] [214]
[214]
We now claim that $H$ is invariant under $U(\theta)$. [223]
\[ [224]
  U(\theta) H U(\theta)^\dagger = H, [224]
  \qquad \forall \theta \in \mathbb R. [224]
\] [224]
Equivalently, [225]
\[ [226]
  [H,S^z_{\mathrm{tot}}]=0. [226]
\] [226]
[226]
Recall that when two operators commute, we can \emph{simultaneously diagonalize} them \cite[Theorem~1.3.12]{Horn_Johnson_2012}. [239]
[239]
\begin{align*} [239]
 [H, S^z_{\mathrm{tot}}] = \sum_{i}^{N} [\sigma_i^x \sigma_{i+1}^x + \sigma_i^y \sigma_{i+1}^y + \Delta \sigma_i^z \sigma_i^z, \sum_{j = 1}^{N} \sigma_j^z ] [240]
\end{align*} [240]
and since operators on different sites commute, only $j = i$ and $j = i+1$ contribute. So we ought to write [257]
\[ [258]
  \sum_{i}^{N} [\sigma_i^x \sigma_{i+1}^x + \sigma_i^y \sigma_{i+1}^y + \Delta \sigma_i^z \sigma_i^z, \sigma_i^z + \sigma_{i+1}^z  ] [258]
\] [258]
and now using the identity $[AB,C] = A[B,C] + [A,C]B$: [264]
\[ [265]
  [\sigma_i^x \sigma_{i+1}^x, \sigma_i^z + \sigma_{i+1}^z  ] = -2i(\sigma_i^y \sigma_{i+1}^x + \sigma_i^x \sigma_{i+1}^y  ) [265]
\] [265]
\[ [266]
  [\sigma_i^y \sigma_{i+1}^y, \sigma_i^z + \sigma_{i+1}^z  ] = 2i(\sigma_i^x \sigma_{i+1}^{y} + \sigma_i^y \sigma_{i+1}^x  ) [266]
\] [266]
which cancel out. Furtermore, the $z$ spins commute as well. Thus the whole sum is $0$ and we are done. [286]
[286]
In the $\SU 2$ case, we have the generators [294]
\[ [295]
  S_{tot}^\alpha = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \sigma_i^\alpha, \quad \alpha \in \{x,y,z\} [295]
\] [295]
[295]
The representation here is  $U(R) = e^{i\theta n \cdot S_{tot} }$ and the Hamiltonian is invariant under [306]
\[ [307]
  U(R) H U(R)^\dagger = H, \quad R \in \SU 2 [307]
\] [307]
[307]
Since [308]
\[ [309]
  [S_{tot}^x, S_{tot}^y ] = i S_{tot}^z [309]
\] [309]
we need a new operator for the simulatenous diagonalization [318]
\[ [319]
  S_{tot} = \sum_{a \in \{x,y,z\}}^{} (S_{tot}^{a})^2 [319]
\] [319]
and we need to verify this is indeed the correct operator TODO. [331]
[331]
The eigenvalues of $S_{tot}^2$ are  $S(S + 1)$ where  $S$ are the half integers. [343]
[343]
Also we have that [347]
\[ [348]
  (\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes6} \cong V_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\otimes 6} \cong 5 V_0 \oplus 9V_1 \oplus 5V_2 \oplus V_3 [348]
\] [348]
[348]
Now our operator is a morphism in $End(V_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\otimes 6})$ and thus by Schurs lemma\footnote{These are related by a permutation matrix. Proof? Is this the X from \cite{devosTensorKitjlJuliaPackage2025}? } [374]
\[ [375]
  H \in \bigoplus_{S \in 0,1,2,3} Mat_{m_S \times m_S} \otimes I_{2S+1} (\mathbb{C}) \cong \bigoplus_{S \in 0,1,2,3} I_{2S+1} \otimes Mat_{m_S \times m_S}(\mathbb{C}) [375]
\] [375]
[375]
So we expect 20 blocks? [380]
$5$ have dimension $1$, $9$ have dimension $3$, $5$ have dimension $5$ and $1$ has $7$. [396]
[396]
\begin{definition}[Matrix Product State] [399]
 \label{def:MPS} [399]
 A \emph{Matrix Product State} is a quantum state $\ket{\psi}$ with $n$ legs written as the contraction of $n$ trivalent tensors $\{A^{[i]}\}_{i \in [n]}$. Formally this reads [423]
  \[ [424]
    \ket{\psi[A]} [424]
    = [424]
    \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_n} [424]
    \operatorname{Tr}\!\left( [424]
    A^{[1]}_{i_1} [424]
    A^{[2]}_{i_2} [424]
    \cdots [424]
  A^{[n]}_{i_n} [424]
    \right) [424]
    \ket{i_1i_2\cdots i_n}, [424]
  \] [424]
  where $A^{[i]}_{i_{k}} \in \mathbb{C}^{D_i \times D_{i+1} }$. The elements of the collection $\{D_i\}_{i \in [n]}$ is referred to as the \emph{bond-dimensions}. [438]
\end{definition} [438]
Note that this is a state with closed boundaries. If we want open boundaries we have to replace the trace with appropriate end vectors (nice source?). [464]
[464]
\begin{example} [464]
 We can represent each product state $\ket{\varPsi} = \ket{\psi}^{\otimes n}$ as a MPS with bond dimension $1$. [478]
\end{example} [478]
[478]
\begin{theorem}[Fundamental Theorem of MPS] [482]
 If two MPS states generated by $A$ and $B$ respectively. [492]
  Figure out what we can do with this. [500]
  [500]
  Proof \cite{ciracMatrixProductDensity2017},\cite{vercleyenMathematicalStructureTensor2018}, \cite{perez-garciaStringOrderSymmetries2008a}. [501]
\end{theorem}

\section{Fermionic Tensor Networks} [3]
\label{sect:fermionicTensorNetworks} [3]
[3]
Here we follow \cite{bultinckFermionicMatrixProduct2017,gaoFermionicTensorNetwork2025,mortierFermionicTensorNetwork2025} primarily. These papers present the theory of fermionic networks over the category of \emph{super vector spaces}, denoted $\sVect$, which is also equal to a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded Vector space $\gVSpace{\mathbb{Z}_2}$ as we will see in section \cref{???}. Each $V \in \sVect$ admits a decomposition into \emph{odd} and \emph{even} parity sectors [52]
\[ [53]
  V = V_0 \oplus V_1. [53]
\] Denote the tensor product in $\sVect$ by $\sgotimes{\Z_2}$. Since fermions posess a non-trivial \emph{exchange statistic}, i.e. exchanging two fermions incurs a phase factor of $-1$ on the wave function, the graded tensor product encodes this under its canonical braiding \footnote{Check on the Nlab, the proof that this is canonical is quite copmlex?} % Is this braiding already? be carefull here TODO [105]
also called the \emph{Koszul sign rule} [111]
\begin{equation} [111]
 \ket{i} \sgotimes{\Z_2} \ket{j} = (-1)^{\left\vert i \right\vert \left\vert j \right\vert } \ket j \sgotimes{\Z_2} \ket{i}. [112]
\end{equation} [112]

Here, the state is fully characterized by its intermediate indeces $x_1 \ldots x_{n-1}$, so we can choose a basis $\ket{x_1 x_2 \cdots x_{n-1} }$. [49]
[49]
Similar to the Heisenberg-chain\footnote{Note that $\frac{1}{2} \otimes \frac{1}{2} = 0 \oplus 1$ in the Heisenberg $\SU 2$ model.}, the golden chain introduces a Hamiltonian that assigns $-1$ to the interaction $\tau \otimes \tau = 1$ and $0$ to the interaction $\tau \otimes \tau = \tau$. [80]
[80]
We can decompose the whole space $\Hom(\tau^{\otimes n+1}, \tau)$ into the local states [91]
\begin{equation} [91]
 \Hom(\tau^{\otimes n+1}, \tau) [92]
  = [92]
  \bigoplus_{\mathclap{\substack{x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n-1} \\ \text{\color{RoyalBlue}{all admissible paths}}}}} [92]
  \Hom(\tau \otimes \tau, x_1) \otimes \Hom(x_1 \otimes \tau, x_2) [92]
  \otimes \cdots \otimes Hom(x_{n-1} \otimes \tau, \tau) [92]
\end{equation} [92]
with the admissability condition that there are not adjacents $1$ in the sequence of $x_i$s. [108]
[108]
This is evaluated as a $3$ local hamiltonian, as we can decompose the spin chain into local parts where two $\tau$ anyons are adjacent (check how they call it in the paper.). [140]

\] [172]

\[ [111]
  V^{ab} = \bigoplus_{c \in Irr(C)} V^{ab}_c  [111]
\] [111]

\[ [132]
  R : \bigoplus_{c \in Irr(C)} V^{ab}_c  \cong \bigoplus_{c \in Irr(C)} V^{ba}_c  [132]
\] [132]

File: ./chapters/categories.tex

We will now explore how to use category theory to model quantum processes. [13]
We want this to be able to do a list of things. First, given two systems $A$ and$B$, we want the combined system to be an object as well. [43]
Given processes, i.e. operators on each individual system $f : A \to A^\prime$,$g : B \to B^\prime $, there should be a combined process. [59]
Additionally, structures such as entanglement and no-cloning should be readily apparent in this theory. [73]
[73]
Consider the tensor product $\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}$ of vector spaces $V$,$W$. We can define this using a \emph{universal property} [91]
[91]
\subsection{Decompositions for Categorical Networks} [4]
[4]
This chapter generalizes the decomposition in \cite[Equation~27]{singhTensorNetworkStates2012a} to both Fusion Categories and the Representation categories of compact groups. Note that in \cite{devosTensorKitjlJuliaPackage2025}, such a generalization is given for representations of finite groups, which does not include $SU(2)$. However I do not yet know if we should do so, since I not yet sure how to argue the F moves here. If we instead take the deformation $U_q(sl_2)$ we get finiteness (and fusion cats?), unfortunately $U_q(sl_2)$ is not a group. [83]

\begin{lemma} [4]
 \label{lem:IsotopyHelper} [4]
 For a vector space $W$, there is an isomorphism [13]
  \[ [14]
    \bigoplus^m W \simeq \mathbb{C}^m \otimes W. [14]
  \] [14]
\end{lemma} [14]
\begin{proof} [14]
 Let ${e_i}_{i \in [m]}$ be the standard basis on $\mathbb{C}^m$. Let [23]
  \[ [24]
    \Phi : \mathbb{C}^m \otimes W \to \oplus^m W [24]
  \] [24]
  be defined by [27]
  \[ [28]
    \phi(e_i \otimes w) = (0, \ldots , w, \ldots 0  ) [28]
  \] [28]
  and linear, thus [31]
  \[ [32]
    \Phi\left(\sum_{i}^{} c_{i} e_{i} \otimes w_{i} \right) = (c_1 w_1, \ldots , c_m w_m ). [32]
  \] [32]
  is clearly bijective, and we have our desired isomorphism. [41]
\end{proof} [41]
[41]
\begin{lemma} [41]
 Let $D$ be a finite dimensional $k$-vector space and let $V$ be an object of a $k$-linear category $C$. Then [63]
  \[ [64]
    D \otimes V [64]
    \cong [64]
    V^{\oplus \dim D} [64]
  \] [64]
\end{lemma} [64]
\begin{proof} [64]
 Let $n = \dim D$. Take a basis $\{e_i\}$ for D. This yields an isomorphism [76]
  \[ [77]
    D \cong \bigoplus_{i=1}^n k \cdot e_{i} \cong k^n [77]
  \] [77]
  Since in a $k$-linear category the tensor product is additive (should we prove this?), we can distribute [95]
  \[ [96]
    D \otimes W \cong \bigoplus_1^n (k \cdot e_{i} \otimes W) \cong \bigoplus W = W^{\oplus n} [96]
  \] [96]
\end{proof} [96]
[96]
\begin{lemma}[Isotopic Decomposition] [98]
 \label{IsotopicDecomposition} [98]
 Let $C$ be a semisimple $k$-linear category with simple objects $\{R_a\}$. Then every object $V \in C$ admits a canonical decomposition [118]
  \begin{equation} [118]
  V \cong \bigoplus_a D_a \otimes R_{a}. [119]
  \end{equation} [119]
  where we refer to $D_a \coloneqq \Hom_C(R_a, V)$ as the \emph{degeneracy} of the space. [130]
\end{lemma} [130]
[130]
\begin{proof} [130]
 Since $C$ is semisimple, there exist integers $m_a\ge 0$ such that [140]
  \[ [141]
    V [141]
    \cong [141]
    \bigoplus_{a \in L} \bigoplus_{\_ = 1}^{D_a^V} a [141]
    \cong [141]
    \bigoplus_{a\in L} R_a^{\oplus m_a}. [141]
  \] [141]
[141]
  Applying the additive functor $\Hom_C(R_b,-)$ yields [147]
  \[ [148]
    \Hom_C(R_b,V) [148]
    \cong [148]
    \bigoplus_{a\in L} \Hom_C(R_b,R_a^{\oplus m_a}) \cong \bigoplus_{a\in L} \Hom_C(R_b,R_a)^{\oplus m_a}. [148]
  \] [148]
[148]
  Then, by Schurs lemma [152]
  \[ [153]
    \bigoplus_{a \in L} Hom_C(R_b, R_a)^{\oplus m_a} = k^{\oplus m_b} [153]
  \] [153]

\begin{lemma}\label{HomTensorFactorization} [170]
Let $C$ be a $k$-linear category and let $D,E$ be finite-dimensional [182]
$k$-vector spaces. For any objects $R,S\in C$, there is a natural [193]
isomorphism [194]
\[ [195]
\Hom_C(D\otimes R,E\otimes S) [195]
\cong [195]
\Hom_k(D,E)\otimes \Hom_C(R,S). [195]
\] [195]
\end{lemma} [195]
[195]
\begin{proof} [195]
Let $m=\dim_k D$ and $n=\dim_k E$. Proof by isomorphism chains: [203]
$$ [204]
  \begin{aligned} [204]
  \Hom_C(D\otimes R,E\otimes S) [204]
    &\cong \Hom_C(R^{\oplus m},S^{\oplus n}) [204]
    && \text{by \cref{lem:IsotopyHelper}} \\[1ex] [204]
  &\cong \bigoplus_{i=1}^{m} \bigoplus_{j=1}^{n} \Hom_C(R,S) [204]
    && \text{by additivity of $\Hom_C$} \\[1ex] [204]
  &\cong k^{mn} \otimes \Hom_C(R,S) [204]
    && \text{by \cref{lem:IsotopyHelper}} \\[1ex] [204]
  &\cong \Hom_k(D,E)\otimes \Hom_C(R,S) [204]
    && \text{since $\Hom_k(D,E) \cong k^{mn}$} [204]
  \end{aligned} [204]
$$ [204]
(The last as s) [208]
\end{proof} [208]

\begin{definition}[The Category $\Rep_k(G)$] [148]
 Let $G$ be a group and $k$ a field. The \emph{category of linear representations of $G$ over $k$} consists of the following data: [171]
[171]
  \begin{itemize} [171]
  \item \textbf{Objects:} The objects $\Rep_k(G)$ are pairs $(V, \rho_V)$, where $V$ is a $k$-vector space and $\rho_V : G  \to \mathrm{GL}(V)$.  [187]
    \item \textbf{Morphisms:} For any two objects $(V, \rho_V)$ and $(W, \rho_W)$ in $\Rep_k(G)$, a morphism from $V$ to $W$ is a $k$-linear transformation $f: V \to W$ that is $G$-invariant (also called an \textit{intertwiner}). That is, for every element $g \in G$, the following diagram commutes: [227]
    \[ [228]
    \begin{tikzcd} [228]
  V \arrow[r, "\rho_V(g)"] \arrow[d, "f"'] & V \arrow[d, "f"] \\ [228]
  W \arrow[r, "\rho_W(g)"'] & W [228]
    \end{tikzcd} [228]
    \] [228]
    In algebraic terms, $f$ must satisfy the condition: [236]
    \[ f \circ \rho_V(g) = \rho_W(g) \circ f \quad \forall g \in G \] [237]
    The set of all such morphisms is denoted by $\mathrm{Hom}_G(V, W)$. [247]
  \end{itemize} [247]
  We can further endow $Rep_k(G)$ with a monoidal structure: For any two objects $(V,\rho_V), (W,\rho_W)$, their tensor product is in $\Rep_k(G)$ by the diagonal action [271]
  \[ [272]
    \rho_{(V \otimes W)} (g) (v \otimes w) = \rho_V(g)v \otimes \rho_W(g)w [272]
  \] [272]
\end{definition} [272]
[272]
